root.meaning: a name for several round, juicy fruits
root.note: In Nahuatl the red tomato was xītomatl; tomatl alone could mean the tomatillo and similar fruits.

stages.meaning: a soft red fruit eaten as a vegetable

history: Tomatoes came to Europe from Mexico in the 1500s, and their name came with them. The Aztecs spoke Nahuatl, and in Nahuatl tomatl was a name for several juicy fruits; the red tomato was xītomatl. The Spanish made it tomate, and English first used that form too, around 1600. In the 1700s it became tomato, probably because people thought of potato. In Britain you say /təˈmɑːtəʊ/, in the US /təˈmeɪtoʊ/. For a long time many people in northern Europe did not eat tomatoes, because the plant belongs to the same family as some poisonous plants. Italians gave the fruit a poetic name: pomodoro, ‘golden apple’.
historyEinfach: Tomatoes come from Mexico. The Aztecs lived there. In their language, the word was tomatl. The Spanish said tomate. English said tomate too. Later, it became tomato, like potato. In the UK, people say ‘to-MAH-to’. In the US, they say ‘to-MAY-to’.

elsewhere.text: Spanish was the bridge for many words from Mexico: tomate, chocolate, aguacate (avocado) and chile (chilli) all came from Nahuatl into Spanish, and from Spanish into English.
